articles.title: Mocking a Health Check and Readiness Probe That Fails Until the Stub Is Ready
articles.excerpt: Quick answer When a mock server runs in a container or a compose stack, it should expose a health and readiness check just like a real service, and the check should distinguish "process started" from…
articles.body: Quick answer When a mock server runs in a container or a compose stack, it should expose a health and readiness check just like a real service, and the check should distinguish "process started" from "stub ready to serve." A liveness probe that returns 200 the instant the process boots, before the spec is loaded and routes are registered, lets dependent clients send requests into a server that is not actually serving yet, producing connection resets or 404s that look like test flakiness. Model two phases: liveness that the process is up, and readiness that the contract has loaded and the mock can answer, then have orchestration wait on readiness before running tests. Why a single early 200 is misleading A mock server does not become useful the moment its process starts.

articles.title: A catalog endpoint is not a checkout contract
articles.excerpt: A product catalog can tell an agent what exists without giving it any ability to buy. That boundary is easy to miss when discovery documents, action names, and a chat interface appear in the same inte…
articles.body: A product catalog can tell an agent what exists without giving it any ability to buy. That boundary is easy to miss when discovery documents, action names, and a chat interface appear in the same integration. “The agent can search products” is a capability statement. “The agent can complete checkout” is a much stronger contract involving order creation, payment authorization, confirmation, and outcome handling. What the recorded QA run showed A recorded QA run of our gateway discovered five store actions: product search, order listing, order retrieval, order cancellation, and order return. It did not discover an order-creation or checkout action. The UCP discovery document advertised catalog search only and reported no payment handlers.

articles.body: Before I let a folder of mixed uploads go through a batch re-encode, I want to know which files will come out bigger. In a quick run I did with HandBrakeCLI and its Fast 1080p30 preset, a 2,030,217-byte clip became 5,853,449 bytes, and a 22,264,465-byte clip only dropped to 21,772,446. So I wrote a small check that reads a file with ffprobe and says skip or encode, and ran it on five public clips whose numbers anyone can reproduce. The clips are five WebM files (VP8 and VP9) from Wikimedia Commons, not phone footage and not H.264 originals. Everything below is one run on an Apple M4 with ffprobe 9.0.2 and belongs to these five files only. Sizes are plain bytes.

articles.title: Writing code for a computer that is mostly asleep
articles.excerpt: Server software grew up around one assumption: the machine stays awake. People post screenshots of uptime counters in the hundreds of days. Code is written as if that's normal. The process stays up, t…
articles.body: Server software grew up around one assumption: the machine stays awake. People post screenshots of uptime counters in the hundreds of days. Code is written as if that's normal. The process stays up, the connection stays open, the clock ticks along one second at a time and nothing ever stops it. Agents break that assumption, because the computer an agent runs on mostly shouldn't be awake. Watch one work for a while. It sends a prompt off to a model and sits there until the answer comes back. Then it runs the tests and sits there again. Some tool on another company's server gets called, and more sitting. Eventually it wants permission from me, and if I'm in a meeting or asleep, that pause lasts hours.

articles.title: Introducing Quarry: Type-Safe ClickHouse Queries for TypeScript
articles.excerpt: I've been building Quarry, an open-source, ClickHouse-native query builder for TypeScript. We're using it at Bold.org in application services and data-processing jobs. I wanted schema-aware query comp…
articles.body: I've been building Quarry , an open-source, ClickHouse-native query builder for TypeScript. We're using it at Bold.org in application services and data-processing jobs. I wanted schema-aware query composition while keeping @clickhouse/client and direct control over the SQL. The problem isn't writing SQL. It's maintaining queries whose structure varies with application inputs, sharing aggregations across call sites, and keeping manually declared result types aligned with projections. That's what I wanted Quarry to handle. Heavily inspired by Kysely Quarry is heavily inspired by Kysely , which we already use for PostgreSQL at Bold. I like its immutable builders, schema-derived types, and API that stays close to SQL. I wanted that experience for ClickHouse.

Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis. Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping to usher in a Golden Age of innovation and discovery. Johnson is home to America’s astronaut corps, the Mission Control Center, and the teams behind some of humanity’s greatest achievements in space.

articles.body: "Star Trek" celebrated its diamond anniversary last month, marking 60 years since it first aired on NBC on Sept. 8, 1966.
